title: Osmolarity vs Osmolality: Why IV Fluids Come With Both
h1: Osmolarity vs osmolality — clinical concentration units
description: Osmolarity: osmoles per litre of solution. Osmolality: osmoles per kg of water. Plasma is 285–295 mOsm/kg. Confuse the units and IV fluid causes cell damage.

author.name: The Turbo Unit Converter engineering desk

reviewer.name: Turbo Unit Converter editorial review
reviewer.credential: verified against NIST SP 811 and category-specific ISO references

hero: One measures solute per volume; the other per solvent mass. Clinical labs use osmolality (temperature-invariant); pharmacy labels use osmolarity.
body: Osmotic pressure across a cell membrane is driven by the number of dissolved particles per unit of water. Two units capture this — osmolarity and osmolality — and they diverge at high concentration or high temperature.

> Osmolarity: Osm / L of solution
> Osmolality: Osm / kg of water
> 1 Osm = 1 mole of osmotically-active particles
> For 1 mole NaCl dissociating fully: 2 Osm (Na⁺ + Cl⁻)

Osmolality: measured by freezing-point depression, temperature-invariant, standard in clinical labs. Osmolarity: calculated from mass concentrations, convenient for pharmacy labels. Body fluids: 285–295 mOsm/kg is normal serum.

20% mannitol (200 g/L, MW 182) = 1099 mmol/L = 1099 mOsm/L (mannitol does not dissociate). This is roughly 4× serum osmolality — infused too fast, it pulls water out of cells and drops intracranial pressure fast, but overshooting causes acute kidney injury from tubular collapse.
Osm/kg for lab measurements. Osm/L for pharmacy calcs. Serum lives in a tight ±5 mOsm/kg window.

faqs.q: Is there a normal osmolar gap?
faqs.a: Yes — measured minus calculated osmolality is <10 mOsm/kg normally. Elevated gap suggests methanol, ethylene glycol, or other unmeasured solutes.
Yes — D5W (5% dextrose) is 278 mOsm/L, iso-osmotic before metabolism.
